tr.td: Two waves of killings: 1943, after the Italian armistice, and May to June 1945, during the Yugoslav occupation of Trieste and Gorizia
Istria and Dalmatia in 1943; the Trieste and Gorizia area in 1945, including the Basovizza pit near Trieste
Yugoslav communist partisans; the 1997 New York Times report adds that the Yugoslav secret police helped in manhunts
Mostly ethnic Italians, including Fascist officials and soldiers, civilians, priests, and some anti-Fascists
Estimates run from 3,000 to 5,000 (historians, as reported by Osservatorio Antisemitismo) to up to 15,000 (InTrieste); the exiles' association Federesuli says 6,000 to 10,000
"Foiba" is traced to fovea, meaning pit, and refers to karst sinkholes on the Carso between Friuli Venezia Giulia, Istria and Dalmatia (UniD Formazione)
At least 3,500 Trieste residents, plus an unknown number of Yugoslavs, Italians and Germans, according to Allied officers and historians cited by The New York Times in 1997
The Italian right says 20,000 Italians were killed in Trieste; the 1997 New York Times report says most scholars consider this greatly exaggerated
Between 230,000 and 350,000 Italians left (UniD Formazione); historians put the number at about 250,000, Federesuli at 350,000 (AFP)
10 February, the Giorno del Ricordo, set by Law 92 of 30 March 2004
Passed the Camera on 11 February 2004 with 502 votes in favour and 15 against; the Senate approved it on 16 March 2004
Mattarella spoke of the "horror" of the killings in 2021 (Il Globo); Napolitano in 2007 called the foibe "one of the barbarities of the past century" (InTrieste)
Whether the killings were ethnic cleansing, genocide or reprisal violence, and how many died, remains disputed among historians and politicians

content.p: Between 1943 and 1945, during and just after the Second World War, Yugoslav communist partisans killed large numbers of people in the border lands of north-eastern Italy and the Adriatic coast. Most of the dead were ethnic Italians. Many were thrown, alive or dead, into deep karst sinkholes called foibe. The number of victims is still disputed, and the event has become a political football in Italy, in the words of AFP. The Italian state sets aside a national day for it, while Slovenia's government has accused Rome of "unprecedented historical revisionism" over how it is presented.

UniD Formazione traces the word foiba to fovea, meaning pit. In the Italian usage it refers to the karst sinkholes of the Carso, the limestone plateau that runs between Friuli Venezia Giulia, Istria and Dalmatia (UniD Formazione). InTrieste describes the victims being thrown into these deep, narrow sinkholes. Over time the word came to mean the killings themselves, and specifically the two waves of violence that took place in 1943 and in 1945.

The region at the centre of the events had a mixed population of Italians and Slovenes. UniD Formazione ties the tensions to the period after the First World War, when Italy took control of Istria and parts of Dalmatia, and to a Fascist policy in the 1920s and 1930s that forced Italian on the border populations: it banned the Slav languages from schools and public offices, closed minority cultural and religious institutions and repressed dissent (UniD Formazione). Eric Gobetti, a historian who has written a book on the foibe, told AFP that the first wave of killings was "a consequence of violence committed by the Italian Fascists against the Yugoslav national minority, Slovenians and Croats, who after the capitulation of Italy, took revenge" (AFP).

Italy signed an armistice with the Allies in September 1943, and the Fascist state collapsed. The Yugoslav partisans who had occupied much of the Istrian peninsula used that moment to strike. The University of Verona's magazine, Univr, announcing a 2020 lecture by Raoul Pupo, a professor of contemporary history at the University of Trieste, says the killings took place in two precise phases, in autumn 1943 and in spring 1945, and that military personnel as well as civilians were among the victims. Before that, UniD Formazione says, the Italian occupation of Yugoslav territory had been marked by reprisals, deportations and the destruction of villages, and the Fascist policy of waging war on civilians fed hatred of Italians (UniD Formazione).

Gobetti told AFP that the reprisals were "not against all Italians but some Italians who represented the Fascist state" (AFP). UniD Formazione says the victims included Fascist officials and soldiers, but also ordinary civilians, priests, intellectuals and public employees suspected of collaboration. It adds that prisoners were often tortured before being shot, and that many were forced to dig their own graves. The same account says the executions were carried out without fair trials (UniD Formazione).
content.h2: The killings of 1945 in Trieste and Gorizia
content.p: The second wave came as the war ended. In May 1945 Tito's partisans pushed toward Italy, took the Istrian peninsula and moved on Trieste. According to The New York Times, which reported in 1997 on a British-American intelligence file and on Allied investigators, the partisans held Trieste for about 40 days before withdrawing in June. During that time they hunted German soldiers, Italian and Croatian Fascists, and suspected opponents of communism. Scores of accused Fascists were paraded through the streets to Yugoslav military courts, and most were condemned and shot, or thrown alive into gorges and pits (New York Times, 1997).

The Times reported that at least 3,500 Trieste residents were killed and thrown into the foibe of the Carso during the occupation, along with an unknown number of Yugoslavs, Italians and Germans who had come to the city. It added that thousands more were deported and that many of them died in Yugoslav detention camps. Its figures came from Allied officers and historians who had examined the killings (New York Times, 1997). UniD Formazione describes the occupation of Trieste, Gorizia and nearby areas after the end of the war in Europe as a time of further arrests and executions, and notes that some prisoners were sent to a Yugoslav camp at Borovnica, where food shortages, forced labour and mistreatment killed many (UniD Formazione).

The Basovizza pit, a foibe near Trieste, is now a memorial to the victims. A Roman Catholic priest, Don Sceck, told investigators in a British-American intelligence report of September 1945 that 150 fascists were sentenced and then mowed down with machine guns by Partisan troops on 2 May 1945 at Basovizza, and that the corpses were thrown into the pit. The same report quotes him saying the prisoners were questioned in front of the whole populace, which accused them, and that women rushed up to say the men had killed or tortured their relatives (New York Times, 1997).

After Yugoslavia broke with the Soviet Union in 1948, the Western powers, wary of upsetting Yugoslavia, stopped pressing it over the killings. In 1997 the Times reported that a Rome prosecutor, Giuseppe Pititto, had opened a fresh attempt to bring charges against three ex-Partisan officials who lived in Croatia, an attempt that many Slovenes and Croats strongly objected to. Ivan Fumic, who led the Partisan veterans' group in Croatia, argued that the Allies had named about 800 Italian Fascists as war criminals, yet none had gone on trial (New York Times, 1997).

No one has a settled total, and each figure comes with a different author. The Osservatorio Antisemitismo reprint of a 2021 article from a US foreign-affairs magazine says historians put the number of Italians murdered by Yugoslav partisans at between 3,000 and 5,000, and that some victims were officials of Mussolini's regime while many others were ordinary citizens accused of complicity (Osservatorio Antisemitismo). Gobetti told AFP that a "maximum of 5,000" people were killed. Federesuli, an association of exiles, puts the figure at 6,000 to 10,000 (AFP). InTrieste says the exact number of victims is unknown but that there may have been up to 15,000 killed (InTrieste). UniD Formazione gives a range from a few thousand to more than 10,000 and calls the figure hard to establish because of scarce documents, difficulty recovering bodies and the politicisation of the topic (UniD Formazione).

The Times reported that the Italian right claims 20,000 Italians were killed in Trieste, a figure most scholars dismiss as greatly exaggerated, and that the Slovene-speaking minority in Trieste often denies that the killings took place (New York Times, 1997). Pupo, quoted by the Osservatorio reprint, rejects the description of the events as ethnic cleansing and prefers "mass political violence", because the militias targeted Italians they associated with a nation that had oppressed Slavs for decades. The Osservatorio reprint also says researchers disagree with calling the killings genocide, describing them as a war crime with political motives (Osservatorio Antisemitismo).

The killings were followed by a mass departure of Italian speakers from Istria, Fiume and the Dalmatian coast. UniD Formazione puts the number who were forced to leave at between 230,000 and 350,000 (UniD Formazione). AFP reports that for historians about 250,000 people were exiled, while Federesuli gives 350,000. Lorenzo Salimbeni, a Federesuli spokesman, told AFP that some 90 percent of the Italian community left because of the violence imposed by Tito's regime, and that they ended up in refugee camps set up by Italy (AFP). Univr describes the exodus as following the killings and as the forced emigration of most citizens of Italian language and ethnicity from territories that the Italian kingdom had lost to Tito's army and then to Yugoslavia (Univr).

The Osservatorio reprint says that until recently the subject was barely discussed and hardly memorialised in Italy. InTrieste says the Giorno del Ricordo, marked each year on 10 February, was declared in 2004 by President Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, and that it commemorates both the victims of the foibe and the exodus of Italians from Dalmatia and Istria after the war (InTrieste). The law itself, Law 92 of 30 March 2004, says the state recognises 10 February as a day to keep alive the memory of the tragedy of the Italians and of all the foibe victims, of the exodus of people from Istria, Fiume and Dalmatia after the Second World War, and of the wider history of the eastern border. It calls for school activities and for study of the cultural heritage of the Italians of Istria, Fiume and the Dalmatian coast (Filodiritto).

The Camera approved the bill on 11 February 2004 by 502 votes to 15, with 4 abstentions, and the Senate passed it on 16 March 2004 (Filodiritto). AFP reports that the law was passed under Silvio Berlusconi's government but backed by opposition parties, and that the narrative it sets out was then taken up by the media (AFP).

Italian presidents have repeatedly spoken about the victims. In 2007 Giorgio Napolitano called the foibe "one of the barbarities of the past century" (InTrieste). In 2021 Sergio Mattarella spoke of the "horror" of the killings in a ceremony for the victims in Friuli Venezia Giulia, Istria and Dalmatia (Il Globo). InTrieste reports that two years before its 2024 article, Mattarella and Slovenia's president, Borut Pahor, laid a wreath at a foibe memorial at Basovizza (InTrieste).

The memorial has become a political issue. In February 2024 AFP reported that Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government had announced a museum for the victims, and that the Senate speaker, Ignazio La Russa, said the day was a chance to honour those who died "at the hands of the communists". Gobetti and other historians told AFP that the Fascist regime had abused minorities in the region, and that the official story of wholly innocent Italian victims leaves out that history (AFP).

The debate has also crossed borders. AFP reported that in 2019 Slovenia accused Rome of "unprecedented historical revisionism" after Matteo Salvini compared children who died in the foibe with those who died at Auschwitz, and that Slovenia's prime minister of the time, Marjan Sarec, said Fascism had aimed to destroy the Slovenian people (AFP).

In Italy the foibe have also become a dispute about the Holocaust. The Osservatorio reprint describes how a 2021 opinion piece by the art historian Tomaso Montanari, who criticised the use of the memorial, led to attacks from Giorgia Meloni and others, and how a bill sponsored by Brothers of Italy would make foibe denial an offence, as Holocaust denial already is. It also notes a Veneto law that required institutes to describe the killings as genocide with at least 12,000 victims in order to receive public funds (Osservatorio Antisemitismo).

Historians still do not agree on what to call the killings or on how many died. The figures given range from a few thousand, through the up-to-15,000 that InTrieste mentions, to the 20,000 the Italian right claims for Trieste alone, a figure most scholars dismiss as greatly exaggerated (New York Times, 1997). The question of how to classify each wave remains open. Gobetti describes the 1945 killings as closer to a "settling of accounts" between the forces that freed the territory and those who had fought alongside the Nazis (AFP).
